questions.question: I put my buttons in two piles. One pile is round. One pile is square. What rule did I use?
questions.explain: Round and square are shapes, so the rule is shape. The trap is to say colour or size, but those do not separate the two piles.

questions.question: Mom put her spoons in two cups. One cup has big spoons. One cup has small spoons. What rule did she use?
questions.explain: Big and small are about size, so the rule is size. Saying just 'big' only names one group, not the rule.

questions.question: I sorted my blocks into two groups. Group A is red. Group B is green. What rule did I use?
questions.explain: Red and green are colours, so the rule is colour. 'Red' only names one group and does not tell you the rule for both.

questions.question: At school, the teacher put our shells in two boxes. Box 1 has smooth shells. Box 2 has bumpy shells. What rule did she use?
questions.explain: Smooth and bumpy are things you feel with your hands, so the rule is touch. Saying 'smooth' only names one box, not the rule.

questions.question: Dad put his keys on two hooks. One hook has silver keys. The other has gold keys. What rule did Dad use?
questions.explain: Silver and gold are colours, so the rule is colour. 'Silver' only names one hook and is not the rule for both.

questions.question: At the beach, I put my rocks in two buckets. One bucket has flat rocks. The other has pointy rocks. What rule did I use?
questions.explain: Flat and pointy describe shape, so the rule is shape. 'Flat' only tells you about one bucket, not the rule for both.

questions.question: I have 6 red buttons and 4 blue buttons. I put them in two piles. Pile A has all the red ones. Pile B has all the blue ones. What rule did I use?
questions.explain: The piles are split by colour (red versus blue), not by how many buttons each has. 'Red' only names one pile, not the rule.

questions.question: At the craft fair, I put my ribbons in two stacks. Stack A has 4 ribbons. Stack B has 3 ribbons. Stack A is all soft. Stack B is all rough. What rule did I use?
questions.explain: Soft and rough are things you feel, so the rule is touch. The numbers 4 and 3 are just how many, not the sorting rule.

questions.question: My brother said: 'I sorted my shells by colour. One group is smooth. The other is bumpy.' What went wrong?
options: He left out the other group
questions.explain: He said 'by colour' but then described smooth and bumpy, which is touch. The right rule name should match what he actually described.

questions.question: I put 4 circles in one bag and 4 squares in another bag. What rule did I use?
questions.explain: You put circles with circles and squares with squares, so you sorted by shape. Saying 'round' only talks about one group, not the rule for both.

questions.question: Mom put 3 round cookies in one plate and 3 long cookies in another plate. What rule did she use?
questions.explain: Round and long are different shapes, so Mom sorted by shape. 'Round' only names one group, not the rule that separates both groups.

questions.question: I put 4 shiny coins in one cup and 4 dull coins in another cup. What rule did I use?
questions.explain: Shiny and dull show different amounts of shine, so you sorted by shine. 'Shiny' only names one group, not the rule for both groups.

questions.question: At the park, I picked up 8 sticks. I put the straight ones in my left hand and the bendy ones in my right hand. What rule did I use?
questions.explain: Straight and bendy are different shapes, so you sorted by shape. 'Bendy' only talks about one hand, not the rule for both hands.

questions.question: At art class, I put 6 brushes in two cups. Cup A has all the soft brushes. Cup B has all the hard brushes. What rule did I use?
questions.explain: Soft and hard are how brushes feel, so you sorted by feel. 'Soft' only names one cup, not the rule that sorts both cups.

questions.question: I have 8 toy cars. I put the fast ones on the top shelf and the slow ones on the bottom shelf. What rule did I use?
questions.explain: Fast and slow are about speed, so you sorted by speed. 'Fast' only names the top shelf, not the rule for both shelves.

questions.question: I have 9 candies. I put 6 in a red box and 3 in a blue box. The 6 candies in the red box are all hard. The 3 candies in the blue box are all soft. Which rule fits my sorting?
questions.explain: Hard and soft are how candies feel, so feel is the rule. The boxes being red and blue is just the boxes, not how you sorted the candies.

questions.question: I put 8 toys in two boxes. Box A has 3 bears and 2 cats. Box B has 2 cars and 1 boat. I put all the animals in Box A and all the vehicles in Box B. What rule did I use?
questions.explain: Animals and vehicles are different types of things, so you sorted by type. 'Bears' only names some of Box A, not the rule for both boxes.

questions.question: I put 4 red balls and 4 blue balls in two bags. My friend says: 'You sorted by size.' What is wrong with that?
questions.explain: All the balls are the same size, so size does not separate the groups. You sorted by colour (red and blue), not by size.

questions.question: I have 12 stickers. I put 8 in one row and 4 in another row. The 8 stickers in the first row are all stars. The 4 stickers in the second row are all flowers. My sister says I sorted by size. Which rule is actually right?
questions.explain: You put stars together and flowers together, so the rule is shape. Your sister guessed size, but that is not what separated the two groups.
